screens.title: Junos OS Troubleshooting Tools
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll make the Junos OS command-line your primary troubleshooting laboratory. You will learn how to inspect device state with show commands, observe live events with monitor, test reachability with ping and traceroute, and collect full system snapshots for support. These tools let you verify physical links, confirm routing decisions, and capture proof to share with support engineers. For example, you will run a focused show interfaces extensive to confirm whether input or output errors point to a bad cable, then use show route with a protocol filter to confirm where a route is learned. You will also learn simple but powerful output modifiers like | match and | except so you can find the exact line you need in lengthy output. Finally, we will practice a scenario that ties interface checks, routing inspection, and reachability testing together so you can form a hypothesis and confirm it with commands. This chapter matters because a structured CLI approach reduces time-to-resolution and avoids misdiagnosis. As you progress, notice how each command answers a single troubleshooting question and how combining them builds a reliable story about what the device actually sees.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Junos OS Troubleshooting Tools
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Junos OS Troubleshooting Tools

In this lesson you will learn command patterns to diagnose link, routing, and reachability problems and how to gather data for support.

Terminal-first troubleshooting
Overview visualization
SHOW
Inspect state and configuration snapshots used to verify interfaces, routes, and protocol adjacencies.
MONITOR
Observe live events and packet captures to confirm dynamic behavior and transient faults.
TEST
Use ping and traceroute to validate reachability and identify intermediate hops when diagnosing path issues.
Coming up
Live demo: show interfaces extensive
Interpret error counters and link details.
Filtering output
Use | match and | except to find the lines you need.
Explore Key Topics
Interface checks
Use show interfaces extensive to confirm physical and logical health before higher-layer debugging.
Routing verification
show route and protocol filters show you where traffic will be sent and why.
Live monitoring
monitor commands and monitor traffic let you observe events and packets in real time when transient issues occur.
Terminal Demo Preview
user@router> show interfaces ge-0/0/0 extensive
user@router> show route 172.16.1.10
user@router> ping 172.16.1.10 source 192.168.1.1 count 5
user@router> show bgp summary | match "192.168.10.1"
user@router> monitor log messages
These commands form the core demonstration you will follow in the live coding segment, illustrating inspection, testing, and observation patterns.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical skills you can use immediately in an operational environment. First, you will master the most frequently used show commands to read device state quickly and accurately. That includes interpreting interface counters, route entries, and protocol adjacencies so you can form a working hypothesis. Second, you will use monitor commands to observe live events and capture packets or logs when issues are transient or time-based. Third, you will perform reliable connectivity tests with ping and traceroute, including using source options and counts to simulate real flows. Fourth, you will collect full diagnostics using request support information and examine system logs with show log messages so you can provide evidence to support teams. Each objective focuses on a practical task: verify, observe, test, and collect. These are the actions network engineers perform every day. I will give concrete examples and simple mnemonics to remember when each tool is the right choice, and we'll practice a scenario tying them together so you gain confidence in real troubleshooting situations.

screens.title: Objective Details and Mnemonics
screens.narratorSegment: Let's attach simple mnemonics to each objective so you can recall the right tool under pressure. Think: 'See, Watch, Probe, Bundle.' 'See' maps to show commands — you use these when you need a snapshot of the device state. For example, 'show interfaces terse' is a quick glance, while 'show interfaces extensive' is a detailed inspection. 'Watch' maps to monitor — use it when you need to observe events as they happen, such as monitor log messages for interface flaps. 'Probe' maps to ping and traceroute — these simulate and trace traffic paths. Remember to specify source to represent the correct path. 'Bundle' maps to request support information — when you need a single package of operational data to hand to support. I will also point out common errors: assuming a route exists without checking the route table, or capturing full traffic on a busy port without filters. These mnemonics help you choose the first command to run and avoid common mistakes that waste time. Practice these patterns until they become your default checklist during an incident.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Objective Details
Mnemonic cards
SEE
show commands
Snapshot device state: interfaces, routes, protocol adjacencies.
WATCH
monitor commands
Live events and logs for timing-sensitive problems.
PROBE
ping & traceroute
Test reachability and trace path hops with source options.
BUNDLE

Collect a complete snapshot for support analysis.
Common mistakes
  • Assuming a route without checking show route or protocol filters.
  • Capturing full traffic on busy ports without match filters, which can affect performance.
Quick checklist
  1. See: show interfaces / show route
  2. Watch: monitor log messages
  3. Probe: ping/traceroute with source
  4. Bundle: request support information

screens.title: The 'show' family of commands
screens.narratorSegment: The show commands are your first resort for understanding what the device believes about its own state. A show command reads current operational data and presents it as a snapshot, which is why we always run show before making changes. For interfaces, there are two useful forms: show interfaces terse gives a compact row per interface indicating administrative and operational status, while show interfaces extensive provides a deep view including counters, media info, and error statistics. For routing, show route shows the active routes in the routing table; you can filter by prefix or by protocol to focus on a particular path. Protocol-specific show commands, like show ospf neighbor or show bgp summary, summarize adjacency and peering states so you can spot missing neighbors or session states such as Established or Idle. A concrete example: if a workstation cannot reach a server, run show interfaces ge-0/0/0 extensive to confirm the link is up and check for incrementing input errors, then run show route 172.16.1.10 to see whether the route is present and which next-hop is used. A common misconception is to trust only ping results without checking device state; ping can fail for many reasons that show commands will clarify. Key takeaway: show commands answer the question, 'What does the device see right now?'.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Show Commands
Definition

show — read device state

Show commands return a static snapshot of operational data and are used to confirm link status, error counters, routing, and protocol states before any corrective action.

Key examples
show interfaces <name> extensive
Detailed counters, link speed, duplex, and media info — essential for Layer 1/2 diagnosis.
show interfaces terse
Concise status of all interfaces for a quick health check.
show route [prefix] | show bgp summary
Inspect routing table entries and BGP peer states to troubleshoot Layer 3 reachability.
Key Takeaway

Always verify device state with show before making changes. Snapshots reveal counters and states that explain symptoms.

Terminal examples
user@router> show interfaces ge-0/0/0 extensive
Physical interface: ge-0/0/0, Enabled, Physical link is Up
  Link-level type: Ethernet, MTU: 1514
  Input errors: 0, Output errors: 0
  Last flapped: 2d 04:12:33

user@router> show interfaces terse
Interface               Admin Link Proto    Local                 Remote
ge-0/0/0                up    up   inet     192.168.1.1/24
ge-0/0/1                up    down

user@router> show route 172.16.1.10
inet.0: 10 destinations, 10 routes (10 active)
172.16.1.0/24      *[OSPF/10] 00:01:23, metric 20
  > to 192.168.2.1 via ge-0/0/1.0
Concrete example
If the interface shows input errors incrementing, suspect a physical issue before blaming routing.
Misconception
A successful ping does not prove proper device configuration; always confirm routes and interfaces with show commands.

screens.title: show interfaces: terse vs extensive
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between show interfaces terse and show interfaces extensive helps you pick the right level of detail. The terse form is a single-line summary per interface that answers the question, 'Is the interface administratively up and operationally up?' Use terse when you need a rapid inventory or to spot obvious down interfaces across many ports. The extensive form is a detailed diagnostic output that includes link-level information, MTU, media type, input and output error counters, last flap time, and per-protocol information. Use extensive when you see errors, mismatches, or intermittent behavior that terse cannot explain. For example, if the user reports packet loss, start with show interfaces terse to confirm the interface is up. If it is up but errors are suspected, run show interfaces ge-0/0/0 extensive to look for increasing input errors or CRCs. A common mistake is to rely solely on terse and miss counter trends; extensive reveals the counters and timestamps you need. In short: terse for fast triage, extensive for root-cause detail. Practice switching from terse to extensive as a two-step diagnostic habit. show interfaces: terse vs extensive means use terse for quick triage and extensive for deep diagnostics when counters or link details matter.. In practical terms, when to use quick status versus detailed interface diagnostics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Interface Views
Quick view

show interfaces terse

A compact table of every interface showing administrative and link status. Use this for fast triage across many ports.

user@router> show interfaces terse
Interface               Admin Link Proto    Local
ge-0/0/0                up    up   inet     192.168.1.1/24
ge-0/0/1                up    down
When many interfaces exist, terse helps locate obvious administratively down or physically down ports quickly.
Deep view

show interfaces <name> extensive

Shows media, link details, error counters, MTU, VLAN tagging, and timestamps — use when you suspect physical or link-layer problems.

user@router> show interfaces ge-0/0/0 extensive
Physical link is Up
Input errors: 23, Output errors: 0
Last flapped: 00:05:12
If input errors are incrementing, suspect cables, optics, or duplex issues before assuming routing problems.
Example
Terse shows the port is up. Extensive reveals 1000 input errors, indicating a physical fault to investigate.
Pro Tip
Start with terse, then escalate to extensive on the affected interface for efficiency.
Common mistake
Relying only on terse can hide counters that explain intermittent packet loss.

screens.title: Routing checks with show route
screens.narratorSegment: When diagnosing Layer 3 reachability, show route is the command that tells you whether the router has a usable path to the destination and why. The basic show route prefix reveals the route, its active status, age, and the installed next-hop. You can narrow the output by specifying a prefix, for example show route 172.16.1.10, or filter by protocol to see only OSPF-learned entries, like show route protocol ospf. This helps you quickly determine if a route is missing, suppressed, or learned from an unexpected protocol. A concrete walkthrough: suppose a workstation cannot reach 172.16.1.10. Run show route 172.16.1.10 to see if the route exists and which next-hop is used. If the route exists and points to a next-hop via ge-0/0/1, but the interface ge-0/0/1 is down, you have a link-level problem. If the route is missing, check routing protocol adjacencies with show ospf neighbor or show bgp summary. A common misconception is assuming that a route in another VRF or table applies; always verify you are viewing the correct routing table (for example inet.0). Key takeaway: route checks connect symptoms to the path and ownership of the route.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › show route
Code walkthrough

Inspecting the routing table

Use a focused show route with a prefix or a protocol filter to learn where a route comes from and which next-hop is installed.

user@router> show route 172.16.1.10
inet.0: 10 destinations, 10 routes (10 active)
172.16.1.0/24      *[OSPF/10] 00:01:23, metric 20
  > to 192.168.2.1 via ge-0/0/1.0

user@router> show route protocol ospf | match "172.16.1.0/24"
172.16.1.0/24      *[OSPF/10] 00:01:23, metric 20
Supporting notes
  • Active marker '*' indicates an active route used for forwarding.
  • Protocol label shows source, e.g., OSPF, BGP, or static.
  • Next-hop and outgoing interface identify the forwarding path.
Key Takeaway

If a route exists but reachability fails, compare the route's next-hop and interface state to find the broken segment.

screens.title: Protocol checks: show ospf neighbor and show bgp summary
screens.narratorSegment: Protocol adjacencies and peer states reveal whether your routing protocols are exchanging information. show ospf neighbor lists OSPF adjacencies and their state, for example Full or 2-way, so you can tell if a neighbor has completed exchange and is eligible to share routes. show bgp summary summarizes BGP peers and shows the state such as Established, Idle, or Active, and often includes the number of prefixes received. Use these commands when routes are missing or unexpected. Concrete example: if show route shows no OSPF routes for a prefix, run show ospf neighbor to verify the neighbor is Full. If the neighbor is not established, the routing table will not receive those routes. Similarly, if BGP is not Established, you will not see remote prefixes. A common misconception is to assume a protocol session is healthy because physical links are up; protocol state can fail due to authentication, timer mismatches, or configuration differences. Always check the protocol states before modifying forwarding behavior. Key takeaway: protocol checks confirm whether route exchange is occurring and point you to the right troubleshooting domain. Protocol checks: show ospf neighbor and show bgp summary means protocol neighbor and summary commands show whether route exchange is happening and why routes might be missing.. In practical terms, verify adjacencies and peering state to diagnose protocol-level failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Protocol Checks
OSPF

show ospf neighbor

Shows neighbor IPs, state, and adjacency timings. Full adjacency is required to learn LSA-based routes.

user@router> show ospf neighbor
Neighbor ID     Pri State   Dead Time   Address         Interface
192.0.2.2         1 Full    00:00:33     192.168.2.2     ge-0/0/1.0
If the state is not Full, LSAs and routes may not be exchanged; check timers and authentication.
BGP

show bgp summary

Summarizes BGP peers, session state, and prefix counts so you can spot missing or flapping peers.

user@router> show bgp summary
Peer             AS    State    PfxRcd
192.168.10.1     65001 Estab    120
If BGP is not Established, no routes from that neighbor will be installed and prefix counts will be zero.
Example
Missing OSPF routes; show ospf neighbor reveals neighbor in 2-way state instead of Full, indicating adjacency did not complete.
Misconception
Physical link up ≠ protocol up. Protocol state can fail for configuration mismatches even when the link is ready.
Key Takeaway
Always check protocol neighbor and summary outputs to confirm the actual exchange of routes.

screens.title: Monitor commands for live observation
screens.narratorSegment: Monitor commands let you observe events and packets in real time, which is essential when an issue is transient or depends on timing. monitor interface streams live counters that show whether traffic and errors are changing. monitor traffic interface is Junos's built-in packet capture tool similar to tcpdump; it displays packets traversing an interface and supports matching filters to capture only relevant flows. monitor log messages follows system logs as new entries appear. A careful example: if an interface is flapping intermittently, run monitor log messages and watch for messages about link down/up or related protocol events; the timestamps can correlate a user's report to system events. Important safety note: avoid running monitor traffic without filters on busy production ports because full captures can consume C P U and memory. Always apply match filters, for example monitor traffic interface ge-0/0/0 matching "host 10.0.0.1", to capture only the traffic you care about. A common misconception is that monitor is harmless; in high-throughput contexts it can impact performance, so use selective filters and short captures. Key takeaway: monitors are powerful for live diagnosis but must be used with care.

keyIdea.title: Watch live, filter wisely
keyIdea.text: Monitor commands reveal dynamic behavior; always use selective filters for packet captures to avoid performance impact.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Monitor
Real-time observation

monitor interface / monitor traffic

Use monitor commands to follow counters, packets, and log lines as they occur to capture transient events and correlate timestamps.

user@router> monitor interface ge-0/0/0
  packets-in: 100 packets-out: 120
  input-errors: 0 -> 1

user@router> monitor traffic interface ge-0/0/0 matching "host 172.16.1.10"
  12:34:56.789 IP 192.168.1.5 > 172.16.1.10: ICMP echo request
  12:34:56.790 IP 172.16.1.10 > 192.168.1.5: ICMP echo reply
Safety notes
  • Do not capture all traffic on busy ports; use matching filters.
  • Limit capture duration to avoid resource exhaustion.
  • Use monitor log messages to correlate events with timestamps.
Pro Tip

Combine monitor traffic with a focused filter and a short sampling window to capture the relevant session without impacting device performance.

screens.title: Ping and traceroute: probing reachability
screens.narratorSegment: Ping and traceroute are the basic probes you use to confirm reachability and understand the path packets take. Ping sends ICMP echo requests and measures round-trip time and loss; useful options include count to send a specific number of probes and source to specify the outgoing interface or IP address so you replicate client behavior. Traceroute displays each hop between source and destination and the latency to each hop, helping you find the hop where packets stop or are delayed. For example, if you cannot reach 172.16.1.10 from a workstation connected to ge-0/0/0, ping that destination from the router using ping 172.16.1.10 source 192.168.1.1 count 5. If ping fails, run traceroute 172.16.1.10 to see the last responding hop. A common misconception is to run traceroute without considering the device source address; results can differ if route selection uses a different outgoing interface. Another pitfall is interpreting ICMP timeouts as total failure; some devices rate-limit or block ICMP while still forwarding traffic. Key takeaway: use source-aware ping to reproduce client flows and traceroute to find the hop where forwarding fails or becomes slow.

narration.text: Ping and traceroute are the basic probes you use to confirm reachability and understand the path packets take. Ping sends ICMP echo requests and measures round-trip time and loss; useful options include count to send a specific number of probes and source to specify the outgoing interface or IP address so you replicate client behavior. Traceroute displays each hop between source and destination and the latency to each hop, helping you find the hop where packets stop or are delayed. For example, if you cannot reach 172.16.1.10 from a workstation connected to ge-0/0/0, ping that destination from the router using ping 172.16.1.10 source 192.168.1.1 count 5. If ping fails, run traceroute 172.16.1.10 to see the last responding hop. A common misconception is to run traceroute without considering the device source address; results can differ if route selection uses a different outgoing interface. Another pitfall is interpreting ICMP timeouts as total failure; some devices rate-limit or block ICMP while still forwarding traffic. Key takeaway: use source-aware ping to reproduce client flows and traceroute to find the hop where forwarding fails or becomes slow.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Ping & Traceroute
Probe

ping & traceroute usage

Use ping for reachability and latency tests and traceroute to discover the sequence of hops and identify where packets are lost or delayed.

user@router> ping 172.16.1.10 source 192.168.1.1 count 5
5 packets transmitted, 5 packets received, 0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max = 1/2/4 ms

user@router> traceroute 172.16.1.10
 1 192.168.1.254  1 ms
 2 192.168.2.1    2 ms
 3 172.16.1.10    3 ms
Guidance
  • Always set source when necessary to mirror the path taken by the client.
  • Use a count to validate intermittent problems over multiple probes.
  • Interpret traceroute results considering routers may deprioritize or block ICMP.
Key Takeaway

Ping verifies reachability; traceroute locates the failing hop. Use source options to produce meaningful results.

screens.title: Collecting diagnostics: request support information and logs
screens.narratorSegment: When a problem is complex or you need to involve vendor support, use request support information to gather a comprehensive bundle of the device's operational state. This command collects configuration, routing tables, interface statistics, logs, and more into a single file you can share with support. Before running it, be aware of privacy and size considerations; the file may contain sensitive data. Complement this with show log messages to read system logs on the device. Logs often contain the first clues — timestamps of interface flaps, process restarts, or security policy hits that preceded a failure. For example, if users report intermittent outages, check show log messages for entries around the reported time to see if an interface flapped or if a routing process restarted. Always combine logs with state commands: a log entry that an interface went down should be verified by show interfaces extensive to inspect counters and last flap time. A common misconception is that request support information replaces the need to interpret output; it merely packages data. Key takeaway: collect a support bundle for external analysis and read logs to build a timeline of events before changing configuration.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Diagnostics & Logs
Collect

request support information

Packages device operational data into a file for support. Use when an incident requires deeper analysis by vendor engineers.

Note
Ensure you review for sensitive data and follow your organization's procedures before sending the bundle.
Inspect

show log messages

Read system logs to find events that correlate with user-reported issues and construct a timeline of what changed and when.

user@router> show log messages | match "ge-0/0/0"
Oct 10 12:03:21 router mgd[12345]: Interface ge-0/0/0: link down
Oct 10 12:03:25 router mgd[12345]: Interface ge-0/0/0: link up
Concrete workflow
1) show log messages to get timestamps, 2) show interfaces extensive for counters, 3) request support information if needed for external analysis.
Misconception
Assuming request support information will explain the issue without you building the timeline first delays diagnosis.
Key Takeaway
Collect a bundle for support but build a local timeline from logs and state before submitting it.

screens.title: CLI Output Modifiers: filter and refine
screens.narratorSegment: Large command outputs can hide the one line you need. Junos CLI output modifiers let you reduce noise and focus on relevant data. The pipe match operator filters lines that contain a pattern, which is ideal when you know a string to search for, for example show bgp summary | match "192.168.10.1" to find a specific neighbor. The pipe except operator excludes lines matching a pattern, useful to remove constant, unhelpful lines. The find operator jumps to the first occurrence of a pattern allowing quick navigation. The count operator gives you a line count which can be handy to check the size of an output, for example counting how many routes match a filter. display detail expands brief fields into full details for commands that support it. A concrete example: show route protocol ospf | match "172.16.1.0/24" will show only OSPF entries for that prefix. A common mistake is over-relying on match patterns that are too broad and accidentally hiding results; use specific strings or anchor portions of the output when possible. Key takeaway: learning to filter effectively saves time and reduces cognitive load when working with verbose outputs.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Output Modifiers
Filters

| match, | except, | find, | count

Pipe modifiers reduce output to the lines you care about or present it in a different form. They are essential for efficient troubleshooting in long outputs.

| match <pattern>
Show only lines that include the pattern.
| except <pattern>
Exclude lines matching the pattern.
| find <pattern>
Jump to the first occurrence of a pattern.
| count
Return the number of lines in the output; useful for quick sizing checks.
Examples
Practical command examples to narrow focus quickly.
show bgp summary | match "192.168.10.1"
show route protocol ospf | match "172.16.1.0/24"
show interfaces | except "up\s+up"  # find non-up interfaces
show log messages | match "ge-0/0/0" | count
Be specific with patterns and validate results; overly broad matches can hide the data you need.
Key Takeaway

Filtering is a habit: craft concise patterns and combine modifiers to focus your investigation and save time.

Practicing this sequence helps you avoid common mistakes like assuming a route exists without checking the routing table or performing unfocused packet captures. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll make the Junos OS command-line your primary troubleshooting laboratory. You will learn how to inspect device state with show commands, observe live events with monitor, test reachability with ping and traceroute, and collect full system snapshots for support. These tools let you verify physical links, confirm routing decisions, and capture proof to share with support engineers. For example, you will run a focused show interfaces extensive to confirm whether input or output errors point to a bad cable, then use show route with a protocol filter to confirm where a route is learned. You will also learn simple but powerful output modifiers like | match and | except so you can find the exact line you need in lengthy output. Finally, we will practice a scenario that ties interface checks, routing inspection, and reachability testing together so you can form a hypothesis and confirm it with commands. This chapter matters because a structured CLI approach reduces time-to-resolution and avoids misdiagnosis. As you progress, notice how each command answers a single troubleshooting question and how combining them builds a reliable story about what the device actually sees.

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical skills you can use immediately in an operational environment. First, you will master the most frequently used show commands to read device state quickly and accurately. That includes interpreting interface counters, route entries, and protocol adjacencies so you can form a working hypothesis. Second, you will use monitor commands to observe live events and capture packets or logs when issues are transient or time-based. Third, you will perform reliable connectivity tests with ping and traceroute, including using source options and counts to simulate real flows. Fourth, you will collect full diagnostics using request support information and examine system logs with show log messages so you can provide evidence to support teams. Each objective focuses on a practical task: verify, observe, test, and collect. These are the actions network engineers perform every day. I will give concrete examples and simple mnemonics to remember when each tool is the right choice, and we'll practice a scenario tying them together so you gain confidence in real troubleshooting situations.

Let's attach simple mnemonics to each objective so you can recall the right tool under pressure. Think: 'See, Watch, Probe, Bundle.' 'See' maps to show commands — you use these when you need a snapshot of the device state. For example, 'show interfaces terse' is a quick glance, while 'show interfaces extensive' is a detailed inspection. 'Watch' maps to monitor — use it when you need to observe events as they happen, such as monitor log messages for interface flaps. 'Probe' maps to ping and traceroute — these simulate and trace traffic paths. Remember to specify source to represent the correct path. 'Bundle' maps to request support information — when you need a single package of operational data to hand to support. I will also point out common errors: assuming a route exists without checking the route table, or capturing full traffic on a busy port without filters. These mnemonics help you choose the first command to run and avoid common mistakes that waste time. Practice these patterns until they become your default checklist during an incident.

The show commands are your first resort for understanding what the device believes about its own state. A show command reads current operational data and presents it as a snapshot, which is why we always run show before making changes. For interfaces, there are two useful forms: show interfaces terse gives a compact row per interface indicating administrative and operational status, while show interfaces extensive provides a deep view including counters, media info, and error statistics. For routing, show route shows the active routes in the routing table; you can filter by prefix or by protocol to focus on a particular path. Protocol-specific show commands, like show ospf neighbor or show bgp summary, summarize adjacency and peering states so you can spot missing neighbors or session states such as Established or Idle. A concrete example: if a workstation cannot reach a server, run show interfaces ge-0/0/0 extensive to confirm the link is up and check for incrementing input errors, then run show route 172.16.1.10 to see whether the route is present and which next-hop is used. A common misconception is to trust only ping results without checking device state; ping can fail for many reasons that show commands will clarify. Key takeaway: show commands answer the question, 'What does the device see right now?'.

Understanding the difference between show interfaces terse and show interfaces extensive helps you pick the right level of detail. The terse form is a single-line summary per interface that answers the question, 'Is the interface administratively up and operationally up?' Use terse when you need a rapid inventory or to spot obvious down interfaces across many ports. The extensive form is a detailed diagnostic output that includes link-level information, MTU, media type, input and output error counters, last flap time, and per-protocol information. Use extensive when you see errors, mismatches, or intermittent behavior that terse cannot explain. For example, if the user reports packet loss, start with show interfaces terse to confirm the interface is up. If it is up but errors are suspected, run show interfaces ge-0/0/0 extensive to look for increasing input errors or CRCs. A common mistake is to rely solely on terse and miss counter trends; extensive reveals the counters and timestamps you need. In short: terse for fast triage, extensive for root-cause detail. Practice switching from terse to extensive as a two-step diagnostic habit. show interfaces: terse vs extensive means use terse for quick triage and extensive for deep diagnostics when counters or link details matter.. In practical terms, when to use quick status versus detailed interface diagnostics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When diagnosing Layer 3 reachability, show route is the command that tells you whether the router has a usable path to the destination and why. The basic show route prefix reveals the route, its active status, age, and the installed next-hop. You can narrow the output by specifying a prefix, for example show route 172.16.1.10, or filter by protocol to see only OSPF-learned entries, like show route protocol ospf. This helps you quickly determine if a route is missing, suppressed, or learned from an unexpected protocol. A concrete walkthrough: suppose a workstation cannot reach 172.16.1.10. Run show route 172.16.1.10 to see if the route exists and which next-hop is used. If the route exists and points to a next-hop via ge-0/0/1, but the interface ge-0/0/1 is down, you have a link-level problem. If the route is missing, check routing protocol adjacencies with show ospf neighbor or show bgp summary. A common misconception is assuming that a route in another VRF or table applies; always verify you are viewing the correct routing table (for example inet.0). Key takeaway: route checks connect symptoms to the path and ownership of the route.

Protocol adjacencies and peer states reveal whether your routing protocols are exchanging information. show ospf neighbor lists OSPF adjacencies and their state, for example Full or 2-way, so you can tell if a neighbor has completed exchange and is eligible to share routes. show bgp summary summarizes BGP peers and shows the state such as Established, Idle, or Active, and often includes the number of prefixes received. Use these commands when routes are missing or unexpected. Concrete example: if show route shows no OSPF routes for a prefix, run show ospf neighbor to verify the neighbor is Full. If the neighbor is not established, the routing table will not receive those routes. Similarly, if BGP is not Established, you will not see remote prefixes. A common misconception is to assume a protocol session is healthy because physical links are up; protocol state can fail due to authentication, timer mismatches, or configuration differences. Always check the protocol states before modifying forwarding behavior. Key takeaway: protocol checks confirm whether route exchange is occurring and point you to the right troubleshooting domain. Protocol checks: show ospf neighbor and show bgp summary means protocol neighbor and summary commands show whether route exchange is happening and why routes might be missing.. In practical terms, verify adjacencies and peering state to diagnose protocol-level failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Monitor commands let you observe events and packets in real time, which is essential when an issue is transient or depends on timing. monitor interface streams live counters that show whether traffic and errors are changing. monitor traffic interface is Junos's built-in packet capture tool similar to tcpdump; it displays packets traversing an interface and supports matching filters to capture only relevant flows. monitor log messages follows system logs as new entries appear. A careful example: if an interface is flapping intermittently, run monitor log messages and watch for messages about link down/up or related protocol events; the timestamps can correlate a user's report to system events. Important safety note: avoid running monitor traffic without filters on busy production ports because full captures can consume C P U and memory. Always apply match filters, for example monitor traffic interface ge-0/0/0 matching "host 10.0.0.1", to capture only the traffic you care about. A common misconception is that monitor is harmless; in high-throughput contexts it can impact performance, so use selective filters and short captures. Key takeaway: monitors are powerful for live diagnosis but must be used with care.

Ping and traceroute are the basic probes you use to confirm reachability and understand the path packets take. Ping sends ICMP echo requests and measures round-trip time and loss; useful options include count to send a specific number of probes and source to specify the outgoing interface or IP address so you replicate client behavior. Traceroute displays each hop between source and destination and the latency to each hop, helping you find the hop where packets stop or are delayed. For example, if you cannot reach 172.16.1.10 from a workstation connected to ge-0/0/0, ping that destination from the router using ping 172.16.1.10 source 192.168.1.1 count 5. If ping fails, run traceroute 172.16.1.10 to see the last responding hop. A common misconception is to run traceroute without considering the device source address; results can differ if route selection uses a different outgoing interface. Another pitfall is interpreting ICMP timeouts as total failure; some devices rate-limit or block ICMP while still forwarding traffic. Key takeaway: use source-aware ping to reproduce client flows and traceroute to find the hop where forwarding fails or becomes slow.

When a problem is complex or you need to involve vendor support, use request support information to gather a comprehensive bundle of the device's operational state. This command collects configuration, routing tables, interface statistics, logs, and more into a single file you can share with support. Before running it, be aware of privacy and size considerations; the file may contain sensitive data. Complement this with show log messages to read system logs on the device. Logs often contain the first clues — timestamps of interface flaps, process restarts, or security policy hits that preceded a failure. For example, if users report intermittent outages, check show log messages for entries around the reported time to see if an interface flapped or if a routing process restarted. Always combine logs with state commands: a log entry that an interface went down should be verified by show interfaces extensive to inspect counters and last flap time. A common misconception is that request support information replaces the need to interpret output; it merely packages data. Key takeaway: collect a support bundle for external analysis and read logs to build a timeline of events before changing configuration.

Large command outputs can hide the one line you need. Junos CLI output modifiers let you reduce noise and focus on relevant data. The pipe match operator filters lines that contain a pattern, which is ideal when you know a string to search for, for example show bgp summary | match "192.168.10.1" to find a specific neighbor. The pipe except operator excludes lines matching a pattern, useful to remove constant, unhelpful lines. The find operator jumps to the first occurrence of a pattern allowing quick navigation. The count operator gives you a line count which can be handy to check the size of an output, for example counting how many routes match a filter. display detail expands brief fields into full details for commands that support it. A concrete example: show route protocol ospf | match "172.16.1.0/24" will show only OSPF entries for that prefix. A common mistake is over-relying on match patterns that are too broad and accidentally hiding results; use specific strings or anchor portions of the output when possible. Key takeaway: learning to filter effectively saves time and reduces cognitive load when working with verbose outputs.

Let's summarize three essential concepts you should retain. First, show commands are your snapshot tool: use show interfaces, show route, and protocol-specific show commands to learn what the device sees at the moment. Second, monitor commands let you observe live behavior and capture packets or logs as events occur; use match filters when capturing traffic to avoid performance impact. Third, use ping and traceroute with appropriate source options to replicate user paths, and collect request support information plus logs when you need to involve support. These concepts form a repeatable workflow: inspect state, observe live events, probe reachability, and collect evidence. Practicing this sequence helps you avoid common mistakes like assuming a route exists without checking the routing table or performing unfocused packet captures. Keep these ideas in mind as mental shortcuts when you enter the CLI under pressure.

This quick reference distills the chapter into three command groups and a short checklist you can mentally run during an incident. Group one: show commands — use show interfaces terse/extensive, show route, and protocol show commands to inspect current state. Group two: monitor commands — monitor interface, monitor traffic with matching filters, and monitor log messages to observe events in real time. Group three: probes and data collection — ping with source/count, traceroute for path analysis, and request support information plus show log messages for evidence gathering. Your checklist: first, verify interface link and error counters; second, check routing tables and protocol adjacencies; third, probe reachability with source-aware ping and traceroute; fourth, monitor logs or traffic if the issue is transient; finally, collect request support information only after you build a timeline and scrub sensitive data.
